en: Preface to the New Edition of the *Jingtu Cheng'en Ji* (Collection on Receiving Grace in the Pure Land):
The *Cheng'en Ji* consists of the words of Dharma Master Miaoneng, who, with a humble mind dedicated to the Way, spoke of recognizing and repaying the grace he had received.

Thus, from beginning to end, there is nothing that does not praise the ultimate Pure Land, express profound devotion to the Master, and encourage one’s own true faith and practice, as well as the direct revelation of one’s faults through a sincere mind;
these words may truly be called a painful whip for awakening the ignorant and a compassionate vessel for crossing the sea of suffering.
The Dharma Master was pure and sincere by nature, possessing innate roots of faith. Even during his time as a Confucian, he saw...
One must certainly pay homage to the Buddha; one should joyfully prostrate upon meeting a monk. Thus, regarding the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land, one may attain such deep faith and diligent practice.
Reflecting that the Pure Land teaching perfectly accords with the needs of the current age, he resolved to develop the Great Mind and exerted his utmost strength to propagate it.

Whenever he encountered someone, he invariably exhorted them to recite the Buddha’s name ten times every morning and to keep count of their recitations. At one time, those who attained rebirth in accordance with these teachings were beyond counting.

Case: There were three people who listened to the Dharma Master’s words; they practiced the ten recitations while keeping count, never wearying until the end of their lives, and all attained rebirth in the Pure Land.
This is what I have personally heard and seen. At Rui County’s Changning Temple, Master Chaozong, three days prior [to his passing]...
Knowing in advance that his time had come, he distributed his robes and scriptures among his relatives and friends.

On the third day, he invited the assembly to recite the Buddha’s name together, and after burning a single stick of incense, he passed away. At Guanghui Temple in Pingyi, Master Jinjing, seven days prior, knew in advance that his time had come;

he therefore requested his pure friends to observe a seven-day retreat (*qijiu*), while he himself observed a vow of silence and joined them in the recitation of the Buddha’s name. Upon reaching [the seventh day]...
On the seventh day, he sat upright and passed away with a joyful countenance. A layman named Huang Maosen, a neighbor of Changning Temple, offered this praise at the time of his death:
"Master Miaoneng showed me that if one truly knows the excellence of the Western Land, even if invited to serve as a king, one would certainly refuse to go.
Indeed, indeed! He further exhorted his wife and children to be diligent in their mindfulness."

The Buddha, having thus uttered the name of the Buddha, passed away. I have briefly recorded these three cases to clarify that those who are karmically suited for the Pure Land and experience the spiritual efficacy of holding the name do so entirely through the power of the Dharma Master’s great vow to propagate this path.

As the Great Master Jianmi stated regarding the Dharma-gate of the Ten Recitations: "This is an indispensable practice for the Pure Land; even those who recite the Buddha's name many times should likewise [practice it]."
Practice this. Master Ouyi said: "Although there are many methods of Buddha-recitation, holding the name is the most simple and convenient.

Although there are many ways to hold the name, keeping count is the most stable and reliable. A practitioner who walks the path in truth does not seek something different from that of ordinary men and women.
Looking now at these three people, there is nothing particularly extraordinary; they simply recited the name ten times while keeping count.
Thus it is known that the merit of recording the count of ten recitations is unspeakably, unspeakably vast.

I, for my part, am deeply ashamed of my own inferiority and have constantly harbored anxiety and doubt. What great fortune it is to hear this essential scripture! Each time I read it, it is as if the clouds part to reveal the bright moon.
In the height of my joy and relief, I have resolved to raise funds for the carving of this [image].

With you as my pure friend, I pray that all who see or hear of this may emulate the Dharma Master’s faith and the Elder’s devotion, so that they may surely attain single-minded mindfulness of the Buddha and be swiftly reborn in the Western Land.
May this serve to repay the words spoken when you gathered blood drop by drop out of gratitude.

The Preface to the New Edition of "Essential Readings for the Lotus School" Faith, aspiration, and the recitation of the Name constitute the most supreme expedient for swiftly escaping the cycle of saṃsāra. Lingfeng said:

"If one's faith and aspiration are not genuine, then even if one maintains 'single-mindedness without distraction,' one will still fail to attain rebirth. Conversely, if faith and aspiration are fierce and keen, then even with a distracted mind..."
If one recites the Buddha’s name, one will certainly attain rebirth in the Pure Land. Chewu said:

"Simply maintain the two dharmas of faith and aspiration constantly within your mind, like a loyal minister receiving the secret edicts of a sagacious sovereign, or a filial son receiving the solemn commands of a compassionate father.
Whether the recitation is frequent or infrequent, it constitutes the primary cause for rebirth. Therefore, know that upholding the Name with faith and aspiration is the essential core of practice."

One must not treat this with negligence. Compiled by the Great Master [Yunqi] Zhuhong, this "Essential Reading for the Lotus School" focuses exclusively on the single method of upholding the Name through faith and aspiration;
it deeply accords with the intent of the *ekavyūha-samādhi*.

It not only enables sentient beings burdened by many obstacles to ascend directly to the stage of non-retrogression, but also allows those filled with doubt to gain faith and courage. Truly, it is a compassionate vessel across the ocean of suffering.

It is the sun of wisdom for the dark thoroughfare [of ignorance]. Furthermore, he composed a preface in one chapter, wherein he unified within a single introduction the thoroughgoing compassionate heart of Śākyamuni, the universally pervasive great vows of Amitābha, the essential framework of the Pure Land, and the wondrous secret of reciting the name.
Not only are his words concise and his meaning comprehensive, but he has also left no residue of the profound purport of the Pure Land. I—[the author]—...
Upon reading it for the first time, my joy exceeded all expectations. It was like a poor man finding treasure, or like one in darkness finding a lamp.

Although books on the Pure Land are as numerous as mountains, among them there are none that lack the suspicion of being either deficient or excessive. Only this single work is most pertinent to the present age; it is perfect in every way.
It is like an arrow that inevitably hits the string, or medicine that precisely matches the ailment. I have named it "The Essential Reading. What more need be said?
I am hesitant; I request that you circulate this immediately to establish pure conditions for future encounters. The Master said, "These texts were compiled haphazardly;

what benefit would circulation bring? It will merely serve as a whip for myself. Because [the requester] pressed him earnestly and did not cease, he finally entrusted me with the task of proofreading and editing it for publication.
My wish is that all who share our aspiration will read it together, clearly understanding its meaning, giving rise to faith and making vows, thereby initiating wondrous practice.

Thus one may swiftly escape saṃsāra and forever attain the stage of non-retrogression; there is nothing that surpasses this. I have respectfully appended these few words as a colophon to mark my joy in the Dharma. Thus it is said.
The Preface to the Western Path states that the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* says: "In the Dharma-ending age, among billions upon billions of people who practice, it is rare for even one to attain the Way;

only by relying on the mindfulness of the Buddha can one achieve liberation. This is because the cultivation of the other paths relies entirely upon one's own power to transcend the three realms; first, one must repent of...

Regarding present karma: one must exhaust all afflictions (*kleśa*). If present karma is not repented, then even the slightest trace of the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana* and *vitarka*) will remain unexhausted;
consequently, birth-and-death in segmented portions (*paricchinna-jāti-maraṇa*) will not cease, and one will be unable to escape the Land of Common Dwelling (*sahā-loka-dhātu*).

Therefore, it is said that among billions upon billions of people who practice, rarely does one attain the Way. Only by reciting the Buddha’s name and seeking rebirth in the Pure Land can one rely on the Buddha’s power to transcend the Triple World (*tridhātu*) horizontally.
There is no need to repent for past karma, nor is it necessary to sever the afflictions (*kleśa*). From this shared world, one is born into that shared world;

once born in that land, the very roots of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) are forever severed. Therefore, it is said that by relying solely on the mindfulness of the Buddha (*nien-fo*), one may attain liberation.
Thus, the Venerable Shandao said: "To cultivate other practices is circuitous and difficult to accomplish; only this Dharma-gate swiftly transcends [birth and death]."
Regarding birth and death, it is further said: "There is only the path of practice; simply recite the name of Amitābha Buddha.

How much more so in this degenerate age, when strife is rampant and false teachers preach the Dharma as numerous as the sands of the Ganges! If one abandons this simple and direct expedient means, how could one not be deluded?
Out of devotion to the Great Master [Shandao], I have respectfully adhered to this intent, compiled the sincere words of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, and composed these four [chapters].

This work consists of eighteen verses, supplemented by the recording of various texts as evidence. It presents the guide to the Pure Land with complete transparency and fully reveals the warrant for rebirth there.

Not only are its words incisive and its principles clear, making it easy to ascend to faith and aspiration, but it also enables those with deep obstructions and dull faculties to easily understand and maintain the practice of *nien-fo*.
It is titled *The Direct Path to the West*, and it truly may be called a direct path.
This is the direct path [to liberation]. There were fellow students such as Xīshòu and Xīděng who initiated a campaign to circulate this work.
It is their aspiration that all who see or hear it shall form pure karmic conditions; and that those who believe and those who aspire shall be reborn together in the Land of Bliss.

Preface to the *Record of Self-Admonition for the Pure Land*:
The Dharma-gate of the Pure Land universally encompasses all capacities; all who possess faith and aspiration shall attain rebirth there, even unto the moment of death. [...]

Even if one is ultimately oppressed by suffering and can only recite the ten recitations, one will certainly transcend horizontally [to the Pure Land]. Were it not for the ocean of vows of Amitābha, how could this be possible?
This may be called the most perfectly sudden among all sudden teachings, and the foremost expedient among all expedients.
Master Lianxi compiled the *Jingtu Zijilu* (Record of Self-Admonition for the Pure Land), which fully upholds this principle; he composed verses to praise it, bringing forth the power of all Buddhas.
These sincere words are brought forth again and again; the essential instructions of the patriarchs are pointed out one by one.

They extol the wondrous realm of the Western Paradise to the utmost and exhaustively lament the suffering conditions of this Sahā world. Thus, they not only cause those of shallow learning to believe with courage, but also inspire them to act.
Furthermore, it enables those of profound realization to manifest the perfect unity of principle and phenomena; it is truly a great bridge and causeway within the ocean of suffering.
Each time I unroll and read it, my hair stands on end, like one waking from deep sleep at the sound of a sudden clap of thunder, or a dull-witted horse struck by a stinging whip.

Thus, one's joy in purity deepens further, and one's weariness with suffering becomes more urgent. Although various texts on the Pure Land are complete in their manifold excellences, none have ever matched this degree of sincerity in piercing through the maladies of the age;
every sentence flows forth from a heart of compassion, and every word is brought forth by actual practice.
Using this to admonish oneself and others, its utmost earnestness is such that it is hoped those with the karmic affinity to encounter it will give rise to profound faith.
Qingxin, you have made a vow to uphold the Name, swearing never to waver. Even if you encounter a profusion of heterodox teachings, you must not be led astray by them.
Whether in a state of distraction or concentration, do not concern yourself with such distinctions; simply adhere strictly to your daily schedule, never failing for a day throughout your life.
Be diligent and earnest every day, and the lotus blossoms of the Pure Land will flourish and thrive day and night. May those of like mind exert themselves together.

Preface to the Divine Jewel of the Pure Land Dharma Gate The reason the Pure Land Dharma Gate is called the "Divine Jewel" is that the Buddha’s virtues are perfectly interfused and manifest according to the mind, just like a *maṇi* gem which fulfills every aspiration.
As the *Amitābha Sūtra* states: "The ocean of the Buddhas' right and universal knowledge arises from the thoughts of the mind."
Therefore, when one contemplates the Buddha with the mind, this very mind is the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics.

This mind creates the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha. Since it is said that "this mind creates the Buddha" and "this mind is the Buddha," one knows that this mind creates the nine realms and this mind is the nine realms.
Whether mundane or supramundane phenomena, there are none that are not produced by the mind. None.

It is not identical to the mind, yet it is [the mind]. Thus, the *Śūraṃgama-sūtra* says: "Know its fundamental cause; it emerges according to its objects of perception. All phenomena that arise are manifested solely by the mind.
In this way, the empty space of the ten directions and the lands as numerous as motes of dust are all things within the mind.
Apart from the mind, not a single dharma can be found. Therefore, know that the ten periods of time—past, present, and future—and their beginnings and ends [are likewise so].
Without departing from the present thought, boundless lands exist; self and other are not separated by even a hair’s breadth.
The distant reaches of ten trillion lands are precisely the Pure Land of the Mind-only; the eighty-four thousand wondrous marks are none other than the Amitābha of one's own fundamental nature.
Previously, I set aside the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss to speak separately of the Pure Land of the Mind-only, setting aside the myriad...

Virtuous and Compassionate Honored One, you specifically speak of Amitābha as the very nature [of reality]. To turn one’s back on the Compassionate Father of the Land of Bliss and fall into the deep pit of the waters of death—how truly lamentable!
Out of longing for the Great Master [Huiyuan], [the author] completely abandoned old habits and exerted himself to investigate this school.
Seeing the erroneous interpretations of his contemporaries and taking pity on his own past errors, he compiled the sincere words of various sages to elucidate the wondrousness of the One Vehicle.

The essence is thus named "The Divine Pearl of the Pure Land. It is intended for those who practice the path of the Pure Land to realize that the single thought-moment of the present moment possesses immeasurable meanings.

They should have faith that Amitābha’s environment and inhabitants are themselves within the Western Land, and that the environment and inhabitants of the West do not depart from one's own original nature.

When the spirit is turned toward billions of lands, it is truly born within one's own mind; when the physical form is conceived within the nine lotuses, how could this escape the span of a single kṣaṇa?
The essence of the divine jewels and the like resides precisely herein. I, deeply ashamed of my own inferior ignorance, have no words worthy of praise;
I merely record what I heard directly from him to manifest the Master’s resolve. Written by the student of Pure Land practice, Fanghui, in the summer of the Ren-shen year.

Preface to the Newly Carved Edition of *Following the Study of the Pure Land* The single volume of *Following the Study of the Pure Land* is the heartfelt, blood-dripping testimony of Master Liàn-xī, who deeply contemplated the Buddha’s grace.
Within it, he expounds the wondrous principles of the Pure Land exhaustively, leaving nothing unexpressed. Not only are his words true and his practices authentic, but they also...
People easily give rise to deep faith; moreover, the text is concise and the principles are clear, enabling them to readily awaken great vows.

Once faith and vows are complete, then the single practice of reciting the Name becomes spontaneous without effort. Taking the essential purport of the two sutras—*The Sutra on the Ritual of Bowing and Contemplation* and *The Sutra on Entering the Samādhi of Buddha-Recollection*—I shall present them in sequence.
Furthermore, taking the direct path and the opening of the mind, I shall clearly set forth the orthodox tradition of the Pure Land.
This has emerged. Were it not for the direct transmission of a virtuous guide and the firm, secret face-to-face instruction, how could such a thing exist?

A teacher who possesses these two virtues—humility and faith—will surely attain rebirth in the Pure Land and meet the Buddha early. I only wish that those who cultivate pure karma would all follow this example.

Postscript to the "Verses on Opening the Heart":
A Single Verse for Opening the Heart through Nianfo. For those who long for the Great Master [Amitābha] by means of nianfo, there are two kinds of obstacles that prevent the arising of joy.
Indeed, the reason why nianfo fails to produce joy is always because one has not yet attained its subtle essence and does not understand it.
Because there is merit, one becomes greedily attached to the gate of awakening and harbors aversion toward delusive thoughts.

If one can attain the subtle knowledge of merit, then both the gate of awakening and delusive thoughts will be free from anxiety. The Buddha’s name is Merit; it is subtle, wondrous, and inconceivable.

If one can believe in it, then all myriad concerns will be forgotten and a heart of joy will surely arise. Yet every practitioner possesses, from time immemorial, the habitual tendencies of delusive thoughts.
Provided one deeply understands its faults, it will certainly not cause harm. Therefore, one need only censure and abandon it; there is no need to focus intently on its elimination.
The more one tries to eliminate it, the more it increases. These six verses follow one another in sequence; read them with a discerning mind and there will surely be profound benefit.
Reciting the Buddha’s name opens the mind; when the mind is opened, one sees the Buddha. Boundless wondrous meanings are all contained therein. Cultivate purity.

This work must be read. I am ashamed that my karmic obstructions from past lives are so deep and heavy that my studies have yielded no fruit. Fortunately, I encountered Master Lian, who bestowed his teachings upon me through successive encounters.
I now hold fast to the practice of *nien-fo* with firm conviction. Reading these verses today, I have further succeeded in severing two kinds of profound obstructions.
I have deeply received the nourishment of the Dharma, and my gratitude for this virtue is boundless. For this reason, I have resolved to carve this work for circulation.

How could I not celebrate? How could I not rejoice? This debt of grace is such that even grinding my bones to powder and shattering my body would hardly suffice to repay it. Thus, at the inspection...
On the anniversary of the Bodhisattva’s birth, she reverently burned nine incense sticks from her arm and made this vow:
"If Fanghui composes another verse in this lifetime, may I surely fall into hell. She then burned six more incense sticks from her arm as an offering to the Teachers of the Two Lands, praying:

"May the power of the Buddhas protect me, so that until my death I shall never forget even a single name of the Buddha, and in a single moment of thought, may I suddenly give rise to [the aspiration for enlightenment]."
That country shall now repay the Buddha’s kindness and recompense the virtue of my teacher. From this day forward, I shall by no means commit such an offense again.
I have hereby respectfully inscribed these few words upon paper to inform my teacher. As I approach the threshold of this letter, I am overcome with the utmost shame and trepidation.
A Necessary Supplement to the Eight Essentials:
In the autumn of the Guiyou year of the Tongzhi era, while I was within the cloistered quarters of Jingjiao Temple, I read Master Lianxi’s *Eight Essentials of the Pure Land School*.
There was no passage that did not cause my sweat to drench my back; the benefits I derived from them are beyond the reach of words of praise. Therefore—
Suddenly forgetting my own negligence and clumsiness, I followed along and harmonized with it. With deep reverence, I offer twelve incense sticks from my arm to manifest my utmost sincerity.
With prostrations, I respectfully preface this work.
Joyfully.

The ocean of Amitābha’s vows surpasses all common measure; By carrying over one's karma, one transcends horizontally, leaving suffering and toil behind. Even those who have committed the five heinous crimes can turn their minds and be born in the four lands;
By reciting the Buddha’s name eight times, one may behold the three bodies. A thousand sutras offer this as a constant exhortation;
Ten thousand treatises therefore hold it in universal esteem. How fortunate to hear this Perfect and Sudden Dharma! With utmost sincerity and joyful devotion, how could I dare to be negligent?
Though weary of self and ashamed, you left the secular world to join the ranks of the Sangha; yet you remain as deluded as before, enduring bitter hardship.

You constantly pursue empty fame at the expense of true virtue, and always contend for petty gains, thereby endangering your entire being. Having escaped the gates of hell, you still invite further transgression; though you have ascended to the Precious Abode, do not...
Having obtained this treasure, I contemplate with clarity in the still night and give rise to deep renunciation. I vow to maintain the recitation of the Buddha’s name without negligence;

through faith and desire, may I achieve samādhi and escape the clamor of the mundane world. Having exhausted all thieving thoughts, my mind dares not waver. Who can contradict the sincere words of the Buddhas?
Transcending [this world], who can surpass the Vows of Amitābha? Day after day, lotus pedestals meet in the void; moment by moment, his jeweled hand beckons from above the pond.
The merit of holding his name with deep faith is great; boundless karmic offenses are extinguished in a single utterance.

I vow to set a fixed time for reciting the Buddha’s name and sever all emotional attachments. First, by cutting off攀緣 (pān-yuán, clinging to objects), one attains right practice. If one’s resolve and strength are not firm, merit will not manifest;

if the root of craving is difficult to uproot, transgressions are difficult to lighten. When the thought of wearying detachment is fierce, cultivation becomes even more earnest; when the heart of joyful aspiration is true, the Way is attained.

Success is certain. After you have attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), may you extensively open up great vows to deliver those lost in the city of delusion.

By practicing the ten recitations, one will attain rebirth; never doubt this. Relying entirely upon the Buddha’s vow, hasten toward the West. Seek the Land of Ultimate Bliss with resolve; do not let it be in vain.

It is past. To recite the Great Name, do not wait for the time. If you have not yet awakened to the fact that other lands are originally one's own country, how could you know that within one's own nature lies Amitābha?
From this day forward, do not cling to the notion that the land exists only within the mind; by practicing with sincerity, you will ultimately behold the Teacher.

What need is there for other methods when one is single-mindedly seeking the Dharma of birth in the Pure Land of Tranquility? The legacy of Shandao is most worthy of emulation. If one holds fast to this single thought, the home is not far;
if all myriad conditions are severed, the path is not remote. To study extensively in other gates is truly difficult to enter; to practice exclusively in the Pure Land is indeed [the way].
It is easy to transcend. Simply recite the name of Amitābha with no other thoughts; when the time for Bodhi is long, the time for delusion will diminish.

Long mindfulness of the Buddha-dharma makes the gateway inherently easy to transcend. Once you have personally encountered a true teacher, you will never again waver. Even for a brief moment, the merit of prostrating before an image is especially great.

Great indeed! To hold the Name throughout one's life brings even greater merit. Seek it with single-minded devotion and earnest sincerity; let the three minds arise fully, not in a casual or superficial way.
If you can truly establish yourself in firm and diligent practice for a long time, why worry that the path to the Western Land is far?

It is truly lamentable that for so long you have turned your back on your compassionate parents; wandering in exile in a foreign land, your suffering extends over time. Saṃsāra is entirely caused by the burden of worldly attachments;

birth and death both arise from the errors of deluded thoughts. You are constantly assailed by the eight winds that destroy your fundamental resolve, and perpetually summoned by the six thieves that bring about ruin.
In my family, this body must surely return to the Land of Ultimate Bliss. I exhort myself to hold the Name and not allow it to be defiled by blemishes.

Last night, I was moved by the Great Master’s compassionate rescue from suffering and he bestowed upon me these sincere words; my gratitude is inexhaustible. These are truly an excellent remedy for rescuing one from suffering.

I then pasted it beside my seat and constantly maintained awareness and illumination. Suddenly, I recalled Master Zhiyi’s *Ten Doubts* (*Shiyi lun*) and his writings on patience (*kṣānti*) in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
Unconsciously, my five viscera felt as if they were burning; I was filled with shame and wept. Reflecting deeply upon this, I felt both sorrow and joy.
I was sorrowful because evil habits are difficult to eradicate and manifest from time to time; I was joyful because of the clarity [of the teachings].
The Master encountered him and was earnestly instructed and sustained by him. Consequently, he composed four verses to chastise himself with remorse.

He reverently burned nine incense sticks from his own arm as an offering to Amitābha Buddha, to mark this event so that it would not be forgotten. Written in the winter of the Guiyou year at Jingjiao Temple.

I have humbly received Your compassionate virtue and been granted an excellent remedy; engraved upon my bones and inscribed in my heart, how could I dare forget it? A rotten raft may save one from drowning, yet it risks sinking oneself;
a mediocre physician treats illness, yet fears harming the patient. An infant far from its mother will surely suffer; a small bird separated from its branch will certainly meet with calamity.
May I always be able to taste bitter medicine, so that this chronic ailment may be eradicated and I may attain refreshing clarity.
In past lives I lacked wholesome causes, so now my appearance as a monk is both ugly and profound. Though the Buddha-dharma has not yet been mastered, I take particular delight in lecturing;
though human relations should be simple, I instead seek frequent intimacy. Knowing only how to meddle in the affairs of others, I fail to realize that my own mind is constantly deluded.
Fortunate to have received these loyal words of clear instruction, from this day forth I shall completely reform my former conduct.
Reflecting deeply upon these words of admonition, I am truly filled with shame and trepidation. How could my meager strength ever suffice to serve as a vessel for crossing over?

My vows are not firm and I turn with the shifting circumstances; my wild mind has not ceased and is tossed about by the winds. The rope of attachment is thin and the sword of wisdom is dull—how can it cut through? This stubborn horse of delusion is shamed, yet there is no wise strategy to subdue it.
I cry out to Amitābha, seeking his protection, that my long-accumulated habitual tendencies may be swiftly extinguished.

My resolve to retreat into seclusion was originally for the sake of right practice; yet how is it that the teachings and principles have never been clarified? The sages of old possessed virtue and yet concealed it;
today I, being without name, crave fame all the more. Delighting in speech surely disturbs the mind;

yearning for kinsmen makes the Path difficult to accomplish. Turning inward to reproach myself, tears flow from both eyes; I beseech the Compassionate Honored One, praying for rebirth in the Pure Land.
Seclusion and Exhortation, Appended to the Manual for Seclusion:
I originally sought seclusion to avoid the disturbances of human affairs; My original intent was to prevent entanglement with worldly matters.
One should exert effort in the six-syllable Great Name; With simple meals at the three periods of the day, one may follow conditions as they arise.
The nature of consciousness does not disdain bitter soup; what need is there for the sweetness of words to know the mind?
Favorable conditions disturb the mind with many hindrances, while adverse conditions aid the Path with few entanglements.
If one’s attachment to the Dharma is not light, one's practice will not ripen; human sentiments are difficult to thin, and the Way is difficult to perfect.
As fame spreads wider, attachment grows deeper; as gain increases, craving becomes firmer.
To urge others is to fear the bonds of human sentiment; to preach the Dharma is to guard against being pulled by the entanglements of the Dharma.
A leper treating his own sores is truly laughable; a broken boat trying to save those drowning is truly pitiable.
Confessing and Exhorting Myself:

While I was at Mingyin Temple in Yudong, I observed among those studying the Pure Land under Master Lian that there were those who spoke with direct sincerity, confessing their own failings without concealment.
Suddenly, my heart was pierced with sorrow and I was moved by the utmost shame. Only then did I realize, since the time I first left the household life, [how I have failed].
I have been entirely devoid of actual practice, seeking nothing but empty fame. Therefore, whenever I committed a transgression, I concealed it all;

yet when I possessed even slight ability, I exerted every effort to praise myself. Now, wishing to reform my former errors, I have burned forty-eight incense sticks on my arm and openly confessed my sins.
Consequently, I have composed four verses as a severe lash of self-reproach. Written in the winter of the *Ren-shen* year.

To return to secular life after becoming a monk is truly shameful; it is regrettable that my past lives lacked the seeds of goodness. Having just emerged from the gate of suffering, I have again retreated;

on the verge of ascending to the Precious Abode, I suddenly turned back my head. Yet, relying on the Buddha’s power to grant further protection, my heart was moved and my longing for the Way was renewed.
Fortunate to once more don the unsurpassed robe, I vow to uphold the Holy Name and journey toward the West.
I am ashamed that my evil habits from many lifetimes are deep; In my ignorance and delusion, the Way is difficult to accomplish. I have studied the essence of Chan, yet no merit has been achieved;
I have read the scriptures, yet their principles remain unclear. My movements and conduct are coarse—truly loathsome; My speech is harsh and my temperament is indeed contemptible.
Contemplating this matter with a clear mind, tears flow from both eyes; I vow to constantly hold the name of that Buddha.
Karmic consciousness drifts aimlessly, never pausing for a moment. How lamentable that the roots of sin from past lives are so deep!

If an evil thought arises while briefly holding the Name, or if turbid thoughts emerge as soon as one recites the sutra—then by diminishing evil and increasing good, one will ultimately escape suffering;
yet if defilement abounds and purity is scarce, one will surely sink into the abyss. I pray that the Buddha will extend his golden arm and lead me back early to the City of Ultimate Bliss.
The three poisons burn fiercely within my body; I earnestly entreat the Great Compassionate Honored One. Constantly driven by evil gains, I follow the whims of my passions;
constantly pursued by empty fame, I act according to external circumstances. Such conduct leads inevitably to downfall; I must repent to avoid sinking into the depths of suffering.
With forty-eight incense sticks burning upon my arm, I offer them to Amitābha, vowing to be reborn in his Pure Land.

Regarding the thorough rejection of the hindrance of desire: among the roots of birth and death, nothing surpasses the five desires; among the obstacles to spiritual practice, nothing surpasses the five hindrances.
Those who seek rebirth in the Western Pure Land must urgently reject them, so that they may accomplish their goal in a single lifetime and ensure their certain rebirth there. Otherwise—

Greed and craving ceaselessly increase, while obstacles to the Path arise ever more frequently. The sufferings of this Sahā world continue to mount, and the bliss of the Western Land remains ever distant.
The Venerable Nengjing, having read the *Divine Pearl of the Pure Land*, composed these verses. Their language is concise yet their meaning is comprehensive;

they are direct and incisive, encompassing every aspect of the principles of delighting in the Pure Land and loathing the defiled world. They are sufficient to exhort and stir one’s body and mind, enabling the swift accomplishment of rebirth in the Pure Land.
This work on karma is intended for those of like mind; it should be placed at the side of one’s seat so that the sun may shine upon the heart. One must daily examine one’s transgressions:

the causes of good and evil and the fruits of suffering and joy reside solely within the single thought-moment of the individual. If greed or anger arise even for a moment, birth and death will flow forth in vast abundance;
yet, as soon as one calls Amitābha to mind, the lotus flower blazes with light. How can one not be cautious? Written by the fellow student Gu-kun.
The western tower of Mingyinsi Temple:
all manner of desires have long been the source of the deepest calamity, causing people to fall into the depths of samsara for eons. One must urgently recite the Buddha’s name to attain peace.
Nurturing [the mind], one can awaken to the original truth through contact with sensory objects.

When false sounds enter the ears, they disturb the human mind; thus, it is difficult to achieve samādhi, and the harm is profound. If you truly desire to be reborn there, you must hear the wondrous [Dharma].
Dharma! From time to time, mindfully recollect the Buddha; do not be negligent.
To inhale various fragrances through the nose brings deep affliction; boundless fetters arise all at once. You must quickly entrust your physical form to the lotus.
Within, there is another extraordinary fragrance that awakens the roots of goodness;

its flavor is what the foolish crave, yet it is difficult for them to cultivate. Those with true resolve will certainly not seek after worldly tastes, but will instead attain rebirth in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing.
In this land, the *amṛta* (the supreme essence) is ever-present, never ceasing.

Those who are deluded by every sensory contact are truly pitiable; they labor painfully to arrange fine garments and soft textures, yet how could they know the True Suchness (*tathatā*) of the Buddha-land?
The essence itself possesses adornment that follows every thought;

yet greed and the poison of craving destroy people—this is most to be feared. How could the boundless cycle of birth and death ever cease? If one does not seek the Pure Land, there will be no carefree liberation.
Abiding here, when will one emerge from suffering?
The blazing fire of anger burns the forest of virtue; thus, the fruits of the path to Bodhi cannot be realized. Always contemplate the Land of Ultimate Bliss, O worthy ones!
Fellows, you are all people of compassion and forbearance;
yet once the demon of sleep arrives, your spirits vanish. Even if you possess spiritual practice, it will be invaded; quickly recite the name of Amitābha to seek deliverance.
On the path, one should find secure rest within the precious lotus flowers.
To be assailed by restlessness and remorse is also cause for alarm; the suffering born of such regret is even more profound. With a sincere heart, always keep Amitābha in mind.
Buddha, I vow to become a person of joy in the Western Land.
If doubt and skeptical thoughts arise even slightly, the Way will not be accomplished; therefore, the Buddhas offer these profound exhortations. Take the direct path to An-yang (Sukhāvatī).
The Path. It is only by relying entirely on the power of faith that one is able to traverse it.

Regarding the *Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Chewu* concerning the painting of an Amitābha image with blood, there is a poem titled "Painting an Amitābha Image with Blood. Having read it, I was moved; therefore, [I have written this]...
In the winter of the Xinwei year, I resolved to draw this portrait using my own blood. When the layman Wu Juexi saw it, he composed ten poems in praise of it with a sincere heart.
Upon reading them, I was greatly delighted and also wrote ten verses in response to express my humble sentiments.
In sorrow, for many kalpas I have been burdened by my Master; manifold sufferings burn me together, never ceasing for a moment.
Shedding blood to transcribe this true likeness, I have no other vow than to pray that my golden arm may soon be extended to me.
Whenever I think of the Compassionate Honored One, my tears fall in streams; the resentment of parting throughout many lifetimes is difficult to erase.
I have carved my own flesh and shed my blood to paint his true likeness, praying only that I may soon hear the sound of his preaching the Dharma.
The golden countenance, formed by myriad virtues, is depicted with blood; the true body and its ultimate reality are most clearly revealed. May I swiftly extinguish my boundless sins;
upon casting off this retribution body, may I surely attain rebirth.
Piercing my own blood to paint this golden body, it is exactly like the true form of the Buddha, no different. With a heart of utmost sincerity, I take refuge in him always;
may I soon escape the mold of the four great elements.
The blazing inferno of the burning house cannot be dwelt in; the myriad spirits dwell there but briefly, suffering a thousand forms of misery.
With a blood-red heart, cultivate the Buddha-way to transcend birth and death, so as to avoid the wrathful gaze of King Yama.
The Blood Chart depicts that Buddha coming from the east; his true body stands upright upon a jeweled platform. I bow my head and sorrowfully recount the affairs of birth and death;
my mournful cries are so piercing that their resonance is like thunder.
How pitiable that the Lord of Mind is not awake; wandering in foreign lands, he is oblivious to his own numinous spirit. Today, longing for home, he sheds blood from his tongue;
though he attempts to paint that Buddha, how could mere pigments suffice?
The color of the Amitābha painted in blood is renewed; there, upon the pond, he manifests his true body in solemn majesty. I feel deep shame for having long turned my back on the True Father;
who recognizes that from the start, we were never separated by the dust of the world?
The karmic fetters of many lifetimes are extremely difficult to untie; I vow to go to the Precious Pond to cultivate and plant anew.
Splitting open my tongue until crimson blood flows, I shall paint forth the Ancient Tathāgata with utmost sincerity.
I am deeply ashamed of my ignorance and failure to recognize the Truth; Amitābha’s salvation surpasses that of a compassionate parent.
Now, with a single drop of my sincere blood, I shall paint this image of the six-foot body within the Lotus Pond.
The former masters said: "If attachment is not profound, one will not be born in Saṃbhava; if mindfulness is not singular, one will not be born in Sukhāvatī.
To investigate the root of light attachment, nothing surpasses revulsion toward the body. To trace the source of a single thought-moment, nothing surpasses faith in the Buddha.

If one can have deep faith in the Buddha, then mindfulness will become singular of its own accord without being sought. If one truly feels revulsion for the body, then attachment will cease without being sought.
Light and yet self-effacing, you are uniquely able to purify your spiritual friends. Having long cherished this resolve, you have established your practice without ceasing.

Furthermore, you were able to sacrifice your body and draw blood to reverently paint an image of Amitābha, inscribing elegant verses therein to express your joy in the Pure Land and your aversion to the cycle of birth and death.

One can see that your heart of lightness and love has become ever firmer and more courageous; the merit of each single thought becomes increasingly earnest and profound. Truly sincere is this resolve! Although—
Not yet having escaped this defiled land, one is no longer a long-term guest of Saṃbhava; not yet having been born in the Treasure Place, one is already a distinguished guest of Sukhāvatī.
Written by Gu-kun in the Ren-shen year of the Tongzhi era.
The *Sūtra on the Verses of the Ten Kinds of Merit of Mindfulness of the Buddha* states:
"If one can temporarily take refuge in the Triple Gem and uphold the name of even a single Buddha, one shall obtain ten kinds of merit in the present life.
First, throughout the day and night, all the devas and powerful divine generals, with retinues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, will remain hidden to guard [the practitioner]."
1. Protection by the two classes of deities. 2. Constant protection by twenty-five great bodhisattvas, such as Avalokiteśvara and others, as well as by all bodhisattvas.
3. Day and night protection and mindfulness by all Buddhas, and constant reception through the radiance of Amitābha.
4. No malevolent spirits can cause harm; neither venomous snakes, poisonous dragons, nor toxic drugs can take effect. 5. Water, fire, enemies, thieves, and weapons—[cannot harm].

Sixth: They shall not suffer the punishments of the Arrow Prison, nor the death by neck-locks and shackles; their past karma shall be extinguished, their lives from enemies shall be liberated, and there shall be no further retribution.
Seventh: Their dreams at night shall be upright, or they shall behold the sublime and wondrous form of Amitābha. Eighth:
Their minds shall be constantly joyful, their complexions radiant, their physical strength abundant, and all their undertakings auspicious. Ninth: They shall always be [protected] by all the world...
The people of the interval [of time] will respectfully make offerings and joyfully prostrate to them as if honoring the Buddha. Tenth, at the end of life, they will be free from fear;

with right mindfulness manifest before them, they shall behold the holy assembly of Amitābha, who will receive them with golden lotus flowers and lead them to rebirth in the Pure Land, where they will enjoy supreme and wondrous bliss until the end of the future.
Master Tianru said: "These ten kinds of merit are fully recorded in the sūtra, spoken by the Buddha’s own mouth."
I proclaim: it brings benefit both in this life and in future lives. You should simply practice with diligence and harbor no doubts.

Regarding the Dharma gate of Buddha-remembrance (*nienfo*), my ability to rest my mind in fearlessness relies entirely upon this. Furthermore, there are many instances where encountering misfortune has been transformed into good fortune.
Therefore, I have composed these verses for easy recitation.
If a person single-mindedly recollects the name of the Buddha, all the devas will protect and uphold them;
great powerful spirits and their retinues will follow them at all times, never departing.
If a person single-mindedly recites the names of the Buddhas, the Bodhisattvas will, by virtue of this, constantly rescue those who are deluded.
The twenty-five [Bodhisattvas], such as Mahāsthāmaprāpta and Avalokiteśvara, will always follow and protect them, causing their bodhicitta to grow.

If a person single-mindedly recollects the names of the Buddhas, all Buddhas will constantly protect and sustain them by virtue of this; how much more so for one who invokes Amitābha, who will always embrace them.
His radiance is constantly emitted to shatter my delusion.
If a person single-mindedly recollects the Buddha’s name, evil spirits and venomous serpents will all keep their distance; poisonous drugs and venomous dragons shall not cause them harm.
Few people know of such benefits as these.

If a person single-mindedly recites the name of the Buddha, fire, water, thieves, and grievances shall all be dispelled; they shall not suffer untimely death, nor shall they endure shackles or fetters;
even the calamities of war and imprisonment shall be shifted away.
If a person single-mindedly recites the name of the Buddha, their past karma and long-standing transgressions will be completely extinguished.
Enemies who have taken their lives shall obtain liberation, and they will be taught to hold onto one another so that they may be forever separated.
If a person single-mindedly recites the Buddha’s name, they will experience auspiciousness in their dreams at night and be spared from extreme peril;
they may behold the sublime and wondrous image of Amitābha, who personally extends his golden arm to take them by the hand.
If a person single-mindedly recites the Buddha’s name, their physical strength will become full and their actions effective; their complexion will radiate light as impurities are washed away;
and their mind will remain constantly joyful, free from even the slightest doubt.
If a person single-mindedly recollects the name of the Buddha, all people will joyfully follow them, reverently taking refuge in and making offerings to them,
honoring them as they would a Buddha or a teacher.

If a person single-mindedly recollects the name of the Buddha, their fears will be eliminated and their mindfulness will not be deluded. The Holy Assembly and Amitābha will together welcome and guide them;
they shall enjoy bliss in the future, never to be parted.
Do not seek swift signs of efficacy;
do not at all hasten to seek such signs. Be diligent and firm in true faith. When the Buddha’s name is invoked, evil thoughts will diminish.
One’s name shall be inscribed upon the petals [of the lotus]; this may first be celebrated.
Pure in practice, do not hastily seek signs of efficacy; having gained faith, you should maintain long-term aspirations.
If you can hold the Name without even a moment’s pause, why worry that the Compassionate Father will not appear?
Pure in practice, do not seek swift signs of efficacy; simply maintain the recitation of the name without divergent views. Your own progress is known by yourself alone;
if you can persevere steadfastly, it will naturally form a solid mass.
Pure in your practice, do not seek swift signs of efficacy; simply persevere every morning without weariness. Before this life ends, you shall transcend with your karma still intact.
Know that this Dharma is fundamentally not gradual.
Truly believe in the Buddha’s name;
do not doubt that the Buddha’s name is most extraordinary. Whose is it that does not recognize what was personally transmitted from the Golden Mouth?
If one is willing to uphold that Buddha’s great name, one will certainly be reborn in His land at the end of life.
Do not doubt that the Buddha’s name is too extraordinary; all Buddhas universally and extensively praise and proclaim it.
If the sentient beings of the great earth receive and uphold it, every person shall surely go to the Land of Lotus Flowers.
Do not doubt that the Buddha’s name is too extraordinary; the vow-mind of Dharmākara shall never perish.
If even ten recitations can secure rebirth, how much more so when one recites continuously throughout the entire day without ceasing?
Do not doubt that the Buddha’s name is too extraordinary; all the patriarchs have spoken thus.
It is difficult to achieve success by studying other paths in a scattered manner, but by practicing this path with single-minded devotion, one may easily transcend.
In the year of Ren-shen during the Tongzhi era,
while I was at Mingyin Temple in Yudong, I was favored by the Great Master Xi,
who repeatedly explained to me in detail the principle of summoning virtue through one's name. Although my karmic obstacles were deep and heavy, upon hearing this at that time, I felt a surge of joy.

Yul had not yet truly grasped the profound meaning. Fortunately, during the winter of the Guiyou year, while at Gwan-nae in Jeonggyo Temple, he carefully studied the words of the Master and attained a sudden realization of their intent.
He then presented several gāthās, seeking the Master’s certification. The gāthās say:

The great name is raised up, its virtue brilliantly manifest; why must one depart from this to contemplate the Buddha-body? I feel deep shame that my hindrances are profound and delusive thoughts are many;
thus, though face-to-face, we do not truly meet.
Uttering a single great name brings forth a Buddha; its profound and subtle merit is difficult to fathom.
That Shao Kang excelled among all schools was entirely dependent on the power of his great vows made during his causal stage.
I believe deeply in the merit of Amitābha; I shall single-mindedly use his name to benefit all sentient beings.
For this purpose, I will not employ any other expedient means, but vow to recite the Great Name without ceasing its sound.
Once the sublime title is invoked, virtues manifest in equal brilliance; sins are extinguished like sands of the Ganges, and blessings are beyond measure.
If even a moment’s thought brings such benefit, how much more so for those who constantly uphold it and enter the realm of the precious lotus.
Reciting the Buddha’s name with self-reproach cannot eliminate the afflictions of profit, fame, and regret; how then could one hope to dispel them through mere delusive thoughts?
Exhort yourself to recite the Name with diligence, lest you fall into the fire-wheel chariot of saṃsāra.
Deep-seated compassion and long-standing karmic obstructions are extremely difficult to eliminate; yet, meeting Amitābha and his merits dispels them all.
Reciting the Great Name with one voice from the mouth, the lotus buds within the pond become as large as chariots.
The many evil habits accumulated over lifetimes are truly difficult to eliminate; even those who have realized the fruits of the path claim they have not yet fully eradicated them.
Only the skillful means of holding the Name are so great that one can transcend horizontally, carrying one's karma with them, surpassing the excellence of the three vehicles.

The three poisons of sentient beings are fundamentally difficult to eliminate; only by surely proceeding to the Western Land can they be dispelled. By merely holding the name, one will ultimately attain it;
why need one further inquire about the White Ox Cart?
Buddha-remembrance is my own good fortune;
this wondrous essence of Buddha-remembrance is not easily heard. Only through the cultivation of seeds over many lifetimes can one be fit for its perfuming.
Relying on meeting a spiritual friend who personally provides guidance and upliftment, one is finally able to leave the defilements behind at all times.
That Buddha especially pities those in this degenerate age; his golden platform reaches everywhere to receive the ordinary and the humble.
Now that I have fortunately encountered such a Dharma, I shall by no means remain idle or linger further in the East.
The Dharma-gate of the Pure Land is wondrous beyond measure; it perfectly gathers all classes of beings into the lotus palace.
Even those for whom the signs of the fiery chariot appear can, by holding the Name, attain transcendence to the midst of Ultimate Bliss.
In the West lies a Buddha whose bliss is inexhaustible; those born there shall ever behold his golden countenance.
Provided that my present aspiration is earnest, I shall surely enter the precious pond in the future.
I vow to go to the Western Land, for this is my long-standing root of merit; throughout many lifetimes, I have repeatedly received the Buddha’s profound kindness.
